subject: Can you determine the relative influence of each landmark on group differences?

messages.author: 8f308306a17e05c6
messages.subject: Can you determine the relative influence of each landmark on group differences?
parts:
I'm interested in quantifying the influence each landmark has in group differences. I think I have a way to do this. First, I should make it clear I'm self-taught when it comes to stats. Reading this group over the years has been very helpful. But apologies if I betray any misunderstandings or if methods to do this already exist. I would welcome any constructive feedback from the community. 

As a test dataset, I have 189 wings from a species of true bug with wing polyphenism. So large shape differences exist, predominantly in the relative size of the distal part of the wing. I've placed 24 landmarks across the wing. Some are internal (crossveins) but most are semilandmarks along the wing's edge. We can categorize these as long or short wing morphs (based on wing length vs. body length). Size and morph are both predictive factors for wing shape. 

```
              Df     SS      MS     Rsq       F      Z Pr(>F)
log10(Csize)   1 2.7641 2.76408 0.68159 485.203 6.5151  0.001 **
morph          1 0.2316 0.23164 0.05712  40.662 5.8410  0.001 **
Residuals    186 1.0596 0.00570 0.26129
Total        188 4.0553
```

Deformation grids are great for looking at overall shape differences. But I'm thinking it should be possible to ask, which landmarks contribute the variance being associated with a particular factor? I wrote a loop to remove each landmark in turn, repeat the GPA and model building, and record the Rsq for the `morph` factor. (Is this "jackknifing"?) Then, I took the difference in Rsq compared to the original model (with all landmarks). I'm reasoning that greater reduction in Rsq for `morph`, following removal of a landmark, indicates that landmark captures more of the variance associated with differences in the `morph` groups. 

The result is particularly satisfying if I plot the difference in Rsq onto the full landmark positions, as below. Distal is on the right. The costal (or leading) wing edge is up. This also confirmed the intuition that distal landmarks were more responsible for the difference in morphs.  



I was a little surprised to see an increase in the effect size for `morph` when certain landmarks are removed. I'm guessing that may because they capture other aspects of variance (not correlating with morph), and when they're removed a greater total share of variance can be described by `morph`?

Please tell me if this is off-base. For example, I'm not sure Rsq is the best statistic to compare (would Z be preferable?) -- or indeed if there might be good reasons not to do this at all. Or if better approaches exists that I'm not aware of. 

Thank you,
Dave Angelini

messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] Can you determine the relative influence of each landmark on group differences?
parts:
Dave,

 

One of the remaining frontiers of landmark-based morphometric theory is to properly estimate the covariance at each landmark, the covariation of each landmark versus some other factor, or the influence of a particular landmark on some data signal.  Your question, and jackknifed proposal, gets at the last of these. Unfortunately it is just not that simple.


The problem here, is that shape variables derived from landmarks are not independent. Each is interconnected mathematically to the others. This occurs during superimposition. In fact, it was way back in Rohlf and Slice 1990 when this was shown definitively (prior to that others had intuited the same, but their paper shows the issue clearly). Please indulge as I describe what they did, as it is still relevant today.

 

Basically, to know whether one has a reliable estimate of the landmark X coordinate covariance matrix, simulate some data with a known mean, and known covariance matrix. Add random translation, rotation, and scale to each specimen. Perform GPA superimposition and obtain the covariance matrix. Compare them.

 

What they found is that the output does not match the input. This means that the superimposition itself imposes covariance constraints landmark by landmark, which in turn, impose constraints on landmark by landmark variation (or influence) relative to other factors. This happens because GPA uses unweighted least squares estimates of translation, rotation, and scale to arrive at the optimal superimposition. But if, say, nearly all landmarks behave similarly, but there is a ‘deviant’ landmark with large variation in some direction (the Pinocchio effect), it will have an undue influence on the superimposition. Resistant fit and other methods were proposed to get at this with various degrees of success.

 

Ok, thanks for the indulgence; now back to your question. The approach you propose is logical. However, two challenges are: 1) the total variation is not the same when each landmark is removed, so the comparisons of R^2 may not be on common ground, 2) even with removing a landmark, GPA on the rest will have an influence (NOTE: Houle and colleagues proposed a similar thing to yours about a decade ago for assessing the influence of each landmark on the superimposition. You’ve taken that one step further, but it has the same challenges).

 

Basically, the question of individual landmark influence on some pattern is still a challenge to evaluate correctly. When we have a weighted Procrustes (and some have been proposed and some of us are developing other methods), this sort of test will be possible. But we are not there yet I am afraid.   

 

Dean

 

Dr. Dean C. Adams

Director of Graduate Education, EEB Program

Professor

Department of Ecology, Evolution, and Organismal Biology

Iowa State University

https://www.eeob.iastate.edu/faculty/adams/

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Can you determine the relative influence of each landmark on group differences?
parts:
Hi Dave,

I forwarded your question and Dean's response about influential landmarks to my colleague, Dr. Subhash Lele, because I thought with his past and current research he would be able to answer your questions. Below is his response to you. If you have any questions, I encourage you to reach out to Subhash - he is very nice and helpful. 

Hope this helps,

Kathy

Hi Dave and Dean:

 

A colleague of mine forwarded your exchange to me. I read it with interest as it reminded me of a few papers and a book I wrote with Professor Richtsmeier on the statistical analysis of landmark coordinates. The approach is called the ‘Euclidean Distance Matrix Analysis’ (EDMA). It has been cited fairly regularly in the literature but you seem to have missed it. I will not go into the details of EDMA in this response but if you are interested I will be happy to chat with you anytime. We are also about to release an R package to analyze data analysis using EDMA with easy graphics and user-friendly interface.

 

I would suggest that you particularly study the following papers. I will be happy to send you the PDF versions if you want. My email is sl...@ualberta.ca.

 

S Lele (1993) Euclidean distance matrix analysis (EDMA): estimation of mean form and mean form difference Mathematical Geology 25 (5), 573-602

 

In this paper, I show that superimposition approach leads to inconsistent estimation of the mean form. But as shown in the paper, far more devastatingly, the covariance matrix estimate based on GPA has no relationship to the true covariance matrix. I show why that is the case. Particularly see the discussion on pages 594-599 and figures 2 and 3. I pointed out this problem originally in my discussion of Goodall (1991, JRSS-B) paper. The paper provides a full treatment. The problem with GPA has been known at least 27 years but unfortunately has been ignored by the general community in morphometrics. Of course, if one cannot estimate the covariance, it is almost trite to claim that form difference as depicted by the little arrows in Procrustes analysis graphics is also wrong.

 

I would like to mention that we already have a solution for the correct estimation of the covariance matrix. A paper is ready to be submitted and it will be included in the R package EDMAinR (not yet released).

 

S Lele (1991) Some comments on coordinate‐free and scale‐invariant methods in morphometrics

American Journal of Physical Anthropology 85 (4), 407-417

 

S Lele, JT Richtsmeier (1992) On comparing biological shapes: detection of influential landmarks

American Journal of Physical Anthropology 87 (1), 49-65

 

The reason we developed an alternative to the superimposition approach was precisely what you have stumbled across. In scientific analysis, testing for the existence of global difference in shapes or forms is seldom of interest (most of the time, researchers know there is a difference). The question of interest usually is: Where are the differences? The localization of the differences is immensely interesting to biologists because such localization can lead to theories for why the differences are in that location/area. See the discussion in Lele (1991) to understand why superimposition methods fail at this basic task. But to the point that you are struggling with, please see the methodology developed in Lele and Richtsmeier(1991). Of course, now we have a slightly better methodology but the basic idea is the same as that discussed in 1991.

There is much more to EDMA than these papers. You are welcome to contact me if you are interested in further discussions.

 

With best wishes,

 

Subhash Lele

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Can you determine the relative influence of each landmark on group differences?
parts:
Yes, I am aware that some explored various incarnations of EDMA, and that in that work the landmark covariance issue was discussed.  However, one must also know the mathematical critiques of EDMA with examples by Rohlf and others in the mid-1999s for a full understanding of why it is not widely adopted as an approach to shape analysis. 

EDMA is not the solution here.

Dean
